response_text:
## Health in Newfoundland and Labrador, 2022

This is Statistics Canada survey data for Newfoundland and Labrador in 2022, covering people 12 and older, both sexes combined. Four findings:

**Adult obesity — about 42%.** Among adults 18 and over, 41.9% were classified as obese based on their self-reported height and weight (adjusted to correct for the well-known tendency to under-report weight). The survey's margin of error puts the true figure somewhere between 38.9% and 44.9%.

**Youth overweight or obesity — about 38%.** Among youth aged 12 to 17, 37.5% were overweight or obese. This number is flagged "use with caution" — the sample was small enough that the plausible range is very wide, from 26.4% to 50.1%. Treat it as a rough signal, not a precise measurement.

**Arthritis — about 27%.** Just over a quarter of people 15 and older (27.3%) reported having arthritis, with a plausible range of 25.3% to 29.4%.

**Diabetes — about 12%.** Roughly one in eight people (12.4%) reported having diabetes, plausible range 10.6% to 14.5%.

### How to read the ranges

Every percentage comes with a "95% confidence interval" — a low and high bound. Because these figures come from a sample rather than a headcount of every resident, the interval says: if the survey were repeated many times, the true population value would fall inside this range 95% of the time. Narrow ranges (arthritis, diabetes) mean a well-measured estimate; wide ones (youth weight) mean the estimate is shaky.

Statistics Canada also attaches quality flags to values. The only one appearing here is **E — "use with caution,"** on the youth figures. Other flags in their system mark data that is suppressed for privacy, too unreliable to publish, preliminary, or revised.

### One caveat worth noting

The height and weight figures are self-reported, not measured by a clinician. The adult numbers have been statistically adjusted to compensate for this; the youth numbers have not, so they may understate the actual rate.
